h1: 10 Most Popular Restaurants in Sa Kaeo
intro: Sa Kaeo is a border province where the food is more interesting than most people expect. From Vietnamese nam nueng recipes passed down through generations, to crispy snakehead fish along Highway Suwan Sri, and a variety of food at Rong Kluea market, we've picked the 10 spots that Sa Kaeo residents and travelers mention most. Here's where your next meal should be.

blocks.html:
If there's one province in Eastern Thailand where the food tells the best stories, Sa Kaeo is high on the list. This is a border city next to Cambodia, home to the busy Rong Kluea market, with a Vietnamese community that settled in Aranyaprathet decades ago and brought their nam nueng, Vietnamese banh cuon, and kuay jap yawn recipes along with them. Walk into Aranyaprathet or Sa Kaeo town today and you'll find Vietnamese restaurants operating in the genuinely traditional style, alongside bold Isan spots, braised noodle stalls, and a mountain café where you can sit all day.

This list covers the restaurants that have become local legends. Yai Tam is known as the first Vietnamese restaurant in Aranyaprathet — open before Vietnamese food was fashionable anywhere in Thailand — and Yai Tem in Sa Kaeo town has retro décor and live music that bring people back again and again. For bold and savory, Pla Chon Wiset in Watthana Nakhon has been selling crispy snakehead fish for 10 THB a piece, and every table orders them. And Kodang Steak near Rong Kluea is where the younger generation comes for a social-media-worthy steak and durian bingsu. Read through and we think you'll want to drive to Sa Kaeo right away.

blocks.name: Yai Tam Vietnamese Restaurant
blocks.signature: Nam nueng, Vietnamese banh cuon, kuay jap yawn, shrimp skewered on sugarcane, Vietnamese banh xeo crepe
blocks.descHtml:
When people in Aranyaprathet talk about Vietnamese food, the first name that comes up is "Yai Tam" — a restaurant over 60 years old, started by a Vietnamese woman who fled the Indochina War through Cambodia and settled here, then opened the district's first Vietnamese restaurant. The recipe has been passed down to her grandchildren and the restaurant still runs today. It sits in the Vietnamese alley on Mittraphap Road, not far from Rong Kluea market — a perfect stop for anyone who's been shopping and wants a meal with some history, or anyone driving through Aranya who wants the real original article.

The dish nearly everyone orders is nam nueng — wrap the fresh pork roll yourself with rice paper, fresh greens, and dip in the restaurant's proprietary sauce. Then come Vietnamese banh cuon (ban khwan) — soft rice-flour sheets with minced pork filling, clear-broth kuay jap yawn, shrimp wrapped around sugarcane stalks fragrant with fresh prawn paste, and crispy Vietnamese banh xeo crepes with a generous filling. Most reviews praise the fresh ingredients, crispy fried spring rolls, and the distinctive dipping sauce. Some note the flavor leans mild rather than punchy compared to newer Vietnamese places — which comes down to personal taste, but the draw here is the original recipe that's been with the city for generations.

The restaurant is clean, airy, and comfortable, with walls covered in photos of famous visitors — so many it's become a signature feature. Per person runs around 101–250 THB. Set menus covering several dishes are available for anyone who can't decide what to order. Open every day from about 07:30–08:00 through roughly 19:00. Midday is busier. Google rates the restaurant at 4.3 stars from several hundred reviews — a sign it's still popular despite being open so long. For a first visit to Aranya and a taste of Vietnamese food with real roots, this is the place to mark on the map.
blocks.bestFor: First meal in Aranya, paired with a Rong Kluea market visit, tasting authentic Vietnamese roots
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: seafood · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Yai Tem Vietnamese Restaurant
blocks.area: Mueang Sa Kaeo District, Sa Kaeo
blocks.signature: Nam nueng (grilled pork), fried spring rolls / Vietnamese cha gio, Vietnamese banh cuon / banh xeo crepe, Vietnamese food set
blocks.descHtml:
When people in Sa Kaeo talk about Vietnamese food, the first name locals often mention is "Yai Tem" — a long-established restaurant that's been part of the city for decades. It started with Grandma Tem's own traditional Vietnamese recipes, which grew into a legendary provincial institution. Great for anyone arriving in Sa Kaeo for the first time who wants both atmosphere and great food in one place. Works equally well for families or groups of friends — the space is wide, and ordering a set to share across the table is the natural way to do it.

The must-order is nam nueng — grilled pork shaped into round portions, served with soft rice paper sheets, a big basket of fresh greens (refills available), rolled by hand and dipped in the restaurant's clear, seasoning-friendly sauce. Next come the fried spring rolls and cha gio (Vietnamese fried fishcake) that reviewers praise as springy, pleasantly salty, and just the right weight. The banh cuon and ban saew (banh xeo Vietnamese crepe) — thin, crispy shells with a hearty filling — are the snacks many people come back for. For a group, the Vietnamese food set covers all the highlights in one order.

Atmosphere is a selling point on its own. The restaurant is decorated in 80s–90s retro style, filled with antiques, a classic car, vintage display cases, and big trees providing shade — photogenic corners everywhere. Live music plays in the evening. Wide parking, per person around 100–250 THB, snack plates 60–150 THB, the large set around 480 THB — fair value when shared by a group.

Located around Municipal Area 17, Soi 5, Mueang Sa Kaeo District, near Sa Kaeo Hospital. Open daily 10:00–00:00 (closed on the 16th of every month). Worth knowing: when it gets busy, food may come out a little slowly — allow extra time. But between the traditional recipes, the consistently good flavors over so many years, and the atmosphere that's hard to find elsewhere, Yai Tem remains a place people visiting Sa Kaeo stop at without fail.
mustOrder: Fried spring rolls / Vietnamese cha gio (fried fishcake)
Vietnamese banh cuon / banh xeo crepe
blocks.bestFor: First meal in the province, groups and families
blocks.hours: 10:00–00:00 daily (closed on the 16th of every month)

blocks.name: Pla Chon Wiset
blocks.signature: Sun-dried crispy fried snakehead fish, clear-broth tom yum snakehead fish, stir-fried snakehead fish, fermented fish and pla ra chili dip
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving along Highway Suwan Sri through Watthana Nakhon and your stomach starts growling, "Pla Chon Wiset" is the restaurant that locals and passing travelers both point to as the go-to lunch stop. The restaurant started as a small roadside stall in the Ban Huay Chot area selling sun-dried snakehead fish for ten baht a piece, and grew into a large full-service restaurant packed at midday. Great for families, friend groups on the road, or anyone who wants boldly flavored Isan food without the heavy price tag.

The star of the menu is the sun-dried crispy fried snakehead fish — just the right size, fried until the outside is genuinely crispy and the inside is still tender. Pair it with the fermented fish and pla ra chili dip with fresh vegetables, and reviewers unanimously say "ordered by every table." For something hot to drink, the clear-broth tom yum snakehead fish is bright and balanced. Stir-fried snakehead fish loaded with aromatics is the go-to for spice lovers. Round out the table with the fermented fish and pla ra chili dip. Fried chicken marinated and fried crisp, som tam, and tom saeb cartilage are also solid supporting dishes for a full meal.

The atmosphere is an open roadside restaurant with good airflow, plenty of tables, and fast service for anyone in a hurry. Per person runs around 101–250 THB — good value relative to freshness and portions. The main branch is open daily 07:30–17:00. A city branch and Branch 2 at the PTT petrol station across from Makro open until around 20:00 for anyone arriving in the evening.

Worth knowing: midday brings a full restaurant and the fried fish can sell out or involve a wait. Arriving before noon or in the early afternoon is more comfortable. If you want to buy unfried fish to take home, the restaurant vacuum-seals them — they travel well in the car without any smell. An easy souvenir to bring back to Bangkok or home.
mustOrder: Fermented fish and pla ra chili dip
blocks.bestFor: Road-trip meal stop, lovers of bold snakehead fish flavors
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: tom yum · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Amsun Vietnamese Food
blocks.signature: Nam nueng, fresh and fried spring rolls, banh mi, banh chung
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving into Aranyaprathet and want genuine Vietnamese food, Amsun is the first name the locals there will recommend. It's a southern Vietnamese recipe restaurant three generations in the making — started by a grandmother of Vietnamese descent who settled in Sa Kaeo and opened a small shop in 1999, then renovated by her children and grandchildren into an industrial loft style that mixes Vietnamese home character with clean, modern atmosphere. Vintage bicycles and Vietnamese girl paintings decorate the walls. Air-conditioned and comfortable. Works well for groups ordering a variety of things to share.

The must-order is nam nueng — the rice paper is ordered directly from Vietnam, giving it a smooth, slightly chewy texture unlike other places; dip in the restaurant's house sauce slow-cooked from sticky rice. Then come the fresh and fried spring rolls with abundant, crispy vegetables, banh hoi (Vietnamese rice vermicelli with lemongrass pork) which several reviews name as the standout second dish, and banh cuon with thin, soft rice sheets. For something hot, the pork rib pho with slow-cooked fall-apart ribs in rich broth, finished with Vietnamese coffee.

Overall flavors reviewers consistently describe as rounded and balanced, with fresh vegetables and plenty of them. Kitchen is in the front — food comes out hot. Prices start in double digits and go to around 140 THB per dish — fair for made-fresh Vietnamese food. Google gives the restaurant 4.3 stars from over 200 reviews, reflecting a place people return to.

Worth knowing: the restaurant is on a side street off Mittraphap Road next to Krung Thai Bank, and parking is somewhat limited. Service can be slower when busy — allow a bit of extra time. Open daily 09:00–19:00, but closed on the 25th and 26th of every month. Plan ahead to avoid missing it.
mustOrder: Banh hoi (Vietnamese rice vermicelli with lemongrass pork)
blocks.bestFor: Authentic Vietnamese food lovers, groups ordering a variety to share

blocks.name: Keng Tom Tun
blocks.signature: Braised beef noodle soup, khao kha moo (pork leg on rice), chicken noodle soup, tender braised meat
blocks.descHtml:
Drive into Aranyaprathet town and get hungry — "Keng Tom Tun" is one of the first restaurants locals think of. It sits off the bypass road at the new junction, about 100 meters in from the Khlong Hat turn, on the right. The landmark is a large building with plenty of seating and easy parking both front and side. Great for road travelers wanting something warm before pushing on, or families who want space without crowding.

The star dishes match the restaurant's name. Most popular is the braised beef noodle soup — tender meat slow-cooked until it gives way completely. The chicken noodle soup has whole pieces of chicken, not fallen apart. The khao kha moo is described repeatedly in reviews as "meltingly tender without being stringy." The noodles are cooked just right — not mushy, still with a slight chew. The broth has a deep, warm braise fragrance that's comforting. It's home-style provincial cooking you could eat daily.

The restaurant is clean and spacious, surrounded by greenery — easy on the eyes, not cramped. The owner looks after customers well and the vibe is friendly. Prices are typical of a braised noodle shop — a few dozen baht per bowl, filling without breaking the budget. Many regular customers say they return multiple times.

Worth knowing: the restaurant is open during the day 08:00–15:00. If you're planning an evening meal, this place won't be open. Arriving mid-morning to early afternoon gets you the best selection without waiting. A good fit for anyone passing through Aranyaprathet or heading toward Khlong Hat.
mustOrder: Khao kha moo (pork leg on rice)
blocks.bestFor: Morning–midday meal stop while passing through Aranyaprathet

blocks.name: Mi Khao Mi Rao Café, Khao Chakan
blocks.signature: Coffee, green tea, fresh milk, grilled toast with butter, milk, and sugar
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving past Khao Chakan and want a spot to sit with mountain and flower-field views in the same place, "Mi Khao Mi Rao Café" is the answer that fits. The café hides behind Khao Chakan Cave Temple, within the Wood House area — a garden café where the flowers change with the seasons: cosmos, blue salvia, and white pampas grass lining bamboo pathways, with the Khao Chakan mountain range as the backdrop. Better for people who want to sit and sip in a genuinely beautiful setting than an ordinary in-town café.

Drinks reviewers keep ordering are coffee, green tea, fresh milk, and tea — made simply, smooth and balanced, not too sweet. The popular snack mentioned across reviews is grilled toast with butter, milk, and sugar: sweet and crispy in just the right measure, and a great pairing with a cold drink while sitting in the garden breeze. Drinks and snacks are priced reasonably — not café-premium pricing.

What makes the place memorable is the open, airy atmosphere, good air circulation, and photogenic spots distributed throughout the garden: a wooden bridge in the middle of the fields, wooden archways, and swings. Come in the late afternoon and you might catch the bat colony flying out from Khao Chakan Cave at dusk — a sight you won't find at other cafés. The location also connects naturally to a visit to Khao Chakan Cave Temple and the Khao Thalu viewpoint in the same trip.

Worth knowing: the café is in an open outdoor garden, and midday sun is strong — arriving in the morning or late afternoon through evening is more comfortable and gives better light for photos. The beauty of the flower fields depends on the season; some periods have flowers in full bloom, others are between planting cycles. Check the café's page before heading out. Open daily from morning to evening, with convenient parking. A good stop along the way while touring Sa Kaeo.
mustOrder: Grilled toast with butter, milk, and sugar
blocks.bestFor: Café lovers after mountain views and flower fields, morning or late afternoon
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: café · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Phawan
blocks.area: Mueang Sa Kaeo District, Sa Kaeo
blocks.signature: Pork blood soup, red pork and crispy pork on rice, khao kha moo with five-spice braising, old-style coffee
blocks.descHtml:
Phawan is an old shophouse in the center of Sa Kaeo town, on Highway Suwan Sri opposite Wat Sa Kaeo (a Royal Monastery). It's a vintage Chinese-style restaurant that many Sa Kaeo residents say they've been eating at since childhood — open for over 20 years. If you wake up early in Sa Kaeo and want a first meal the way local people actually eat, this place is a strong fit: open from as early as 06:30 (not 07:00 as Google lists it) and open through to around 14:00 every day. Works well for people who like a retro shophouse atmosphere, simple tables and chairs, and one-dish meals that come out fast.

The most talked-about dish is the pork blood soup — real reviews consistently describe a rounded broth, large pork blood pieces, clean offal, and bouncy pork chunks. For rice dishes, try the red pork and crispy pork on rice, or the khao kha moo braised with five-spice — fragrant and properly soft. The crispy pork here gets specific praise for being actually crispy with tender meat. An old-style brewed coffee rounds it all off perfectly in a restaurant like this. Additional stir-fry dishes are available to order alongside.

Prices are very accessible — most people pay under 100 THB per head, plain rice at 10 THB per bowl, and side dishes are generous for the price. Regular customers specifically mention the fast service and consistent flavors across many years. A good fit for people rushing to work or getting on the road early.

Worth knowing: the restaurant is on the main road in a shophouse — limited parking, street-side only. Mornings are busiest especially on holidays. Arriving in the early morning gets you the best seat and a complete menu before things sell out. Phawan has a second branch near Sa Kaeo Hospital on Highway Suwan Sri for anyone on the other side of town.
mustOrder: Red pork and crispy pork on rice
Khao kha moo with five-spice braising
blocks.foodType: Pork blood soup / red pork on rice
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: street food · Charles Haynes / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 2.0)

blocks.name: Ek O Cha
blocks.signature: Khao man kai (Hainanese chicken rice), pork blood stew, khao kha moo
blocks.descHtml:
Ask anyone in Aranyaprathet where to go for breakfast and "Ek O Cha" will come up in the first answers. It's a khao man kai and khao kha moo shophouse restaurant on Ratsadon Utit Road (next to the former BAAC branch), a long-standing name that locals call a legendary restaurant. The atmosphere is a plain shophouse — ordinary tables and chairs, nothing decorated or fancy — but it's been packed since early morning since it opened. A good fit for people who want genuinely delicious food at accessible prices, not a photogenic setting.

The most-ordered dish is khao man kai — large pieces of tender, firm chicken (not beaten flat), plenty of meat, rice cooked to just the right softness. Reviews consistently say the chicken is tender in a dense way, not mushy. Then comes the pork blood stew — large bowl, rounded broth, full portions of meat. And the khao kha moo, cooked to the right softness without going stringy. The crispy pork is also a standout — genuinely crispy with a satisfying edge, slightly salty, pairing well with the dipping sauce. What people mention most is the house dipping sauce — strong flavor with a little heat, works with both the steamed chicken and crispy pork. It's what keeps people coming back.

Prices are very accessible — khao man kai from around 60 THB, most dishes under 100 THB. Three people ordering freely pay around 270 THB combined and leave full — which is why reviews keep saying the quality exceeds the price. This consistent value over many years is what built the loyal following.

Worth knowing: the restaurant is an open-hours place roughly 06:00 to around midday to 13:30 — when items sell out, it closes. Anyone wanting the full menu should arrive early. Peak times have a queue, and the restaurant takes cash only — bring small bills.
blocks.bestFor: Breakfast khao man kai in Aranya town
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: pork leg rice · User:Bi89 / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 3.0)

blocks.name: Krua B-Tiang
blocks.signature: Crab fried rice, fresh nam nam salad, fried spare ribs, o-suan (fried oyster Thai-Chinese style)
blocks.descHtml:
Krua B-Tiang is a long-established Thai-Chinese stir-fry restaurant in the middle of Aranyaprathet market, open for over 30 years — a name that the older generation in Aranya knows well. The restaurant occupies a vintage wooden shophouse with both indoor and open-air seating. A good fit for a proper sit-down meal with family, groups, or travelers passing through Aranya town before Rong Kluea market and the Poipet border, who want consistent, reasonably priced food.

The most-ordered dishes are the crab fried rice — reviewers describe plenty of crab meat and a good wok-fragrance — and fresh nam nam salad (sour, spicy, and just right), crispy fried spare ribs (crispy outside, tender inside), and o-suan (fried oyster Thai-Chinese style) which is hard to find at most restaurants. There's also steamed sea bass with lime, three-flavor fried fish, braised tofu with toppings, hoi jo (crab spring rolls), and plenty of spicy stir-fry options. Reviews lean consistently toward "every dish is good, with a home-style flavor you can't find elsewhere."

Per person runs about 100–250 THB. Feature dishes like the fried spare ribs and o-suan go higher at around 200 THB, but the crab fried rice starts in the early hundreds. Service is attentive, food presentation is clean, credit cards accepted, parking available, and delivery service offered. The restaurant scores 4.3 on Google from real reviews — a sign of long-standing local trust.

Located on Bamrung Rat Soi, in the center of Aranyaprathet market, opposite the Aranyaprathet waterworks, next to a shabu restaurant — easy to find. Open 11:30–20:30 daily. Worth noting: closed on the 1st and 16th of every month, so check before planning your visit. On holidays and for the evening crowd it gets busy — large groups should call ahead to reserve.
blocks.bestFor: Family sit-down meal in Aranya town
blocks.spice: Order to your preferred spice level
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: seafood · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Kodang Steak
blocks.area: Aranyaprathet District (Rong Kluea market), Sa Kaeo
blocks.signature: Beef steak (medium rare), durian bingsu, desserts
blocks.descHtml:
Kodang Steak is a stylishly decorated warehouse-style steak restaurant tucked into the Rong Kluea market area of Aranyaprathet, near the Rong Kluea post office on Si Phen Road. The right place for anyone who's been walking the market all day and wants to sit in an air-conditioned restaurant, eat a proper steak, have a coffee, and finish with something cold and sweet. The menu has solid range — beef steak, pork steak, salmon steak, and bingsu — making it a fit for both families and groups of friends.

The dish people mention most is beef steak. For tender meat, the recommendation is medium rare. Real reviews consistently say the grilling is well-timed, the meat comes out soft and juicy with a sauce that's sweet-sour with a touch of heat — cuts through any richness well. The durian bingsu is the dessert to try: smooth ice, ripe durian at just the right sweetness, a large portion easily shared by several people. There's also pork loin steak at a friendly price point, ribeye, and Norwegian salmon steak for anyone wanting the premium option.

Value is fair for a provincial steak restaurant, averaging 101–250 THB per person. Basic pork steak starts in the low hundreds, while premium beef and the durian bingsu climb a bit with the ingredients. The restaurant is nicely decorated, open and comfortable, free Wi-Fi, credit cards accepted, and pets welcome — a more relaxed stop than sitting at the edge of the market.

The location is a real advantage, right in the Rong Kluea market zone with constant foot traffic. Open Mon–Sat 11:00–21:30, Sun 11:00–22:00. Works as a midday meal after shopping or an evening meal before heading back. Worth knowing: when the market is busy the restaurant fills up — larger groups should allow extra time. And if you like your steak tender, tell the staff the doneness level when you order.
blocks.bestFor: Rest stop after a day at Rong Kluea market, families

blocks.title: What to know before you eat in Sa Kaeo

items.title: A private car is the most practical way to get around
items.text: The restaurants on this list are spread across several districts — Aranyaprathet, Sa Kaeo town, Watthana Nakhon, and Khao Chakan. Grab is sparse in Sa Kaeo. Renting a car or hiring a local day-hire vehicle makes covering all of them much more comfortable.

items.title: Always carry cash
items.text: Street stalls and local restaurants often run on cash only. Some accept PromptPay QR, but not everywhere. Keep small-denomination bills handy — paying for crispy snakehead fish or a noodle bowl at a few dozen baht each goes smoother without needing change.

items.title: Beat the queues by arriving before noon
items.text: Popular spots like Pla Chon Wiset fill up completely at midday and the fried fish can sell out. Arriving before noon gets you a complete menu without waiting. Vietnamese restaurants on long weekends are busy too — allow extra time.

items.title: English menus aren't everywhere
items.text: Most local restaurants here have Thai-only menus. Opening a food photo on your phone or using a translation app to point at dishes works well. Pointing at what the table next door ordered also works perfectly. Sa Kaeo people are warm and happy to recommend.

items.title: Tipping is not expected, rounding up is fine
items.text: Street stalls and local restaurants have no tipping custom — pay the menu price. If you were impressed by the service, rounding up or leaving small change is a kind gesture the restaurant appreciates. Some sit-down restaurants may already include a service charge in the bill.

items.title: Pair your meal with the Rong Kluea market
items.text: Rong Kluea is a large border market in Aranyaprathet worth browsing. Plan a midday meal near the market and stroll to digest afterward. Bring an umbrella or a hat — the sun there is strong.

blocks.title: Planning your day of eating in Sa Kaeo
blocks.html:
If you have one day, use Aranyaprathet as your base — most of the top restaurants cluster here. Start breakfast with khao man kai and pork blood stew at Ek O Cha, then move on to a midday lunch of nam nueng at Yai Tam, the first Vietnamese restaurant in Aranya. In the afternoon, walk Rong Kluea market, then finish with steak and durian bingsu at Kodang Steak.

If you're driving along Highway Suwan Sri, don't miss Pla Chon Wiset in Watthana Nakhon — the crispy fried snakehead fish fills up the restaurant by midday, so arriving before noon is safer, or buy unfried fish vacuum-sealed for the road home. For Sa Kaeo town proper, Yai Tem is the call for an evening meal with retro atmosphere and live music. And if you're passing Khao Chakan, Mi Khao Mi Rao Café is the right stop for coffee with a mountain view before continuing.

blocks.text: Want to eat your way through both days without rushing back? Book a night in Aranyaprathet or Sa Kaeo town — wake up early for nam nueng and explore Rong Kluea market at a comfortable pace.

faq.q: Which restaurant is most famous in Sa Kaeo?
faq.a: By reputation and history, Yai Tam is the most talked-about — considered the first Vietnamese restaurant in Aranyaprathet, open before Vietnamese food was widely known anywhere in Thailand. For snakehead fish, Pla Chon Wiset in Watthana Nakhon is the standout: consistently busy on the highway and a landmark for anyone passing through.

faq.q: What are the signature foods of Sa Kaeo?
faq.a: Number one is Vietnamese food — especially nam nueng, Vietnamese banh cuon, kuay jap yawn, and spring rolls, available at Yai Tam and Amsun in Aranyaprathet and Yai Tem in Sa Kaeo town. Another provincial signature is crispy fried snakehead fish from Pla Chon Wiset, and the variety of food stalls in the Rong Kluea border market area.

faq.q: How much does food in Sa Kaeo cost?
faq.a: Most places are very accessible. A braised noodle bowl at Keng Tom Tun runs around 50–70 THB, and khao man kai or pork blood stew in the old town starts at around 40 THB. Vietnamese restaurants and sit-down dining run roughly 101–250 THB per person. Pla Chon Wiset is famous for the snakehead fish at around 10 THB a piece, with a full meal under 250 THB per person.

faq.q: Do I need to book a table in Sa Kaeo?
faq.a: Street stalls and noodle restaurants like Keng Tom Tun or Ek O Cha are walk-in only. For popular spots during peak hours, like Pla Chon Wiset at midday, the fried fish can sell out — arriving before noon is better than trying to book. For Yai Tam and Yai Tem, if you're coming as a large group or during a long holiday weekend, calling ahead to check table availability is worth it.

faq.q: Which places in Sa Kaeo are open in the evening or late at night?
faq.a: Yai Tem in Sa Kaeo town is open until midnight — a good choice for a long evening meal with live music. The Khao Chakan café Mi Khao Mi Rao is best in the afternoon through evening. Restaurants focused on rice-and-curry and Pla Chon Wiset tend to close in the afternoon — if you're planning an evening meal, focus on the sit-down restaurants and check each one's hours before heading out.
